item.title: Scaling AI Modernisation Means Scaling Decisions, Not Just Code
item.description:
There is a growing assumption in software modernisation that AI will allow us to industrialise the analysis and transformation of existing estates. Give a model a codebase, define the target architecture and increasingly it can analyse, refactor, generate tests and produce a substantial amount of the target implementation.

There is clearly value in that, but the idea becomes much harder when we move from an individual application to an enterprise estate. The problem is not simply that organisations use different technologies. There can be enormous variation between two applications built in the same language, by the same organisation and notionally against the same standards. Years of design decisions, local conventions, framework choices, technical debt, developer preferences and changing architectural standards leave each application carrying part of its own history.

item.title: AI Beside the Critical Path
item.description:
I had a conversation with a client recently that crystallised something I have been thinking about for a while.

Like many organisations, they are asking reasonable questions about the value they are getting from AI. There has been significant experimentation, plenty of interest and no shortage of potential use cases, but there is still a sense that the value being realised does not quite match the scale of the conversation around it.

item.title: If You Keep Looking at Your Toes, You’ll Never See the Horizon
item.description:
I have been working with a couple of teams recently where, despite the problems being quite different, I keep seeing the same behaviour.

They are looking at their toes.

In one case, it is a technical team dealing with a standard security-related change process. There is a substantial amount of work in flight, different kinds of requests are mixed together, and the team is struggling to see what is actually happening across the system. Work enters, progresses through a series of activities and approvals, gets delayed, is picked up again, and eventually comes out the other side. Everyone is busy, but it is remarkably difficult to answer some fairly basic questions: what is holding things up, which work is genuinely complex, where is the constraint, and what could we change to make the whole thing flow better?

item.title: Borrowing Horizons
item.description:
My seven-year-old daughter spends quite a lot of time thinking about the future, usually in the form of questions for me.

“When can I ride a motorbike?” “When can I use that power tool?” “When can I jump off that?”

Sometimes she wants a date. Is it when she’s eight? Ten? A teenager? Sometimes tomorrow seems perfectly reasonable.

What I find fascinating is the ambition behind the questions. She can imagine herself doing almost anything; what she doesn’t yet have is a particularly sophisticated understanding of the risks, dependencies or capabilities involved in getting there. Her horizon is enormous because experience hasn’t yet taught her all the reasons something might be difficult.
